description: We are a hardware-first team of Electronics and Communication Engineering students specializing in embedded systems, custom circuitry, and physical prototyping. While we leverage modern software for data analysis, our core strength lies in building the physical infrastructure that bridges the real and digital worlds—moving from bare schematics to fully functional edge devices.
summary:
To address the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge, we developed the Junior Astronaut Command Deck, an interactive, web-based space survival simulator. STEM education often oversimplifies space exploration or makes it too complex for young learners to enjoy. Our solution finds the perfect middle ground.
In our 10-day orbital simulation, students step into the role of a mission commander. They must manually allocate a drag-and-drop "Command Core" to different engineering stations to balance Power, Food, Radiation Shielding, and Life Support. The game teaches the harsh realities of space travel—such as daily baseline resource drains and unpredictable space hazards like solar flares—forcing kids to make critical engineering trade-offs. For example, boosting hydroponics to grow food will directly drain power and water reserves.
Featuring a 3D orbital background and tactile "emergency override" hardware switches, our simulator makes complex resource management tangible, highly strategic, and incredibly fun for the next generation of space explorers.
details:
What it does & How it works:
The Junior Astronaut Command Deck is a web-based, 3D-integrated resource management simulator. Players take on the role of a mission commander for a 10-day orbital/lunar outpost mission. Using a tactile "drag-and-drop" interface, players assign a Command Core to different engineering stations to generate resources.

Benefits & Intended Impact:
Space STEM education often oversimplifies the brutal realities of space exploration. Our simulator bridges this gap by making engineering trade-offs tangible. If a student wants to grow food, they must sacrifice power and water. By balancing passive daily resource drains and unpredictable space hazards (like solar flares), kids experience firsthand the decisions that determine mission success or failure.

Tools & Languages Used:
We built the simulator using HTML5, Vanilla JavaScript, and Tailwind CSS for the glassmorphism UI. We utilized Three.js to render the live 3D rotating moon and starfield background. The project is hosted and deployed via Vercel.

Creativity & Team Factors:
As a hardware-first team of Electronics and Communication Engineering students, we brought our physical engineering mindset to a software interface. Instead of boring multiple-choice buttons, we designed interactive drag-and-drop power cores and physical-style "Emergency Override" toggle switches to make the web app feel like actual command deck hardware.
